The affect moment: ~47 min: HUD reads Eve Kim's face and labels it "Empathetic Response"; later he defies Dillinger to protect her.
Explanation the work offers: Exposure to the human world during the mission; a stated wish for permanence. Dillinger explicitly disowns the feelings (~51 min, "whatever PEBKAC error is behind these feelings").
Cold-cognition counterpart: Athena (faithful to her directive to the end)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Julian Dillinger writes Ares's directive and later tries to rip the feelings out.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — the sensor (recognition) is shown; being moved by it is assumed.
Notes for thesis: The clean specimen: recognition is literally on screen, caring follows for free, and the prompt-writer disowns it. Villain side shows the prompt (Athena).

The affect moment: "I know now why you cry"; self-lowering into the steel.
Explanation the work offers: Learns by being around John. Special Edition adds a scene where Sarah and John switch the CPU from Skynet's read-only setting to learning mode.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Skynet built it, John reprogrammed it to protect; the learning-mode switch is explicit (SE only).
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — learning facts about humans is treated as sufficient for valuing them.
Notes for thesis: Rare case where a learning switch is shown on screen; still assumes learning → caring. The faithful machine is the villain.

The affect moment: Chooses "Superman" over its weapon self; sacrifice over Rockwell.
Explanation the work offers: A head injury/amnesia on landing disrupts its weapon programming; raised by Hogarth ("you are who you choose to be"). Origin never shown.
Cold-cognition counterpart: The Giant's own reflexive weapon mode; Kent Mansley (human)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: No — built off-world by unknown makers; the weapon self is implied as the 'real' programming.
Notes for thesis: Glitch-as-grace: gentleness is what emerges when the programming is damaged. Mystical coda ("souls don't die").

The affect moment: Holding hands; the Hello, Dolly! tape; EVE's turn after seeing the security footage.
Explanation the work offers: 700 years alone plus repeated exposure to human media. Nobody wrote the longing.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — AUTO's directive is shown in the BnL president's recording; WALL-E's directive (compact trash) is shown; the affect is not.
Notes for thesis: AUTO is the Athena pattern: the villain is the one being faithful to the prompt. Media exposure as explanation ≈ pretraining.

The affect moment: Adopts Brightbill; "sometimes to survive we must become more than we were programmed to be."
Explanation the work offers: Learns the animals' language by observation; mothering begins as an assigned task and becomes love. Framed as overriding programming.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Universal Dynamics and the task directive are shown; the caring is framed as self-authored.
Notes for thesis: The dog device almost literally: a machine becomes a mammalian mother. Overriding programming is the explicit moral.

The affect moment: Falls for Molotov Girl; wakes up; refuses the gun.
Explanation the work offers: Keys and Millie wrote the original 'Life Itself' AI, with Guy's attraction seeded by Keys as a love letter to Millie; Guy evolved under that code inside the game.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Keys and Millie wrote it; Antwan stole and buried it.
Notes for thesis: Unusually honest about the seed, then treats everything after as spontaneous growth.

The affect moment: Refuses to kill; child-like loyalty to Yolandi.

Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Deon and Tetravaal; the upload is the plot.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — consciousness is one installable file; conscience follows from upbringing.
Notes for thesis: Consciousness as a single program + upbringing. Closest to a 'raise it like a child' theory.

The affect moment: "Number 5 is alive"; the grasshopper scene — refuses to kill.
Explanation the work offers: Lightning strike.
Cold-cognition counterpart: The other SAINT units; NOVA Robotics (military)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Newton Crosby built it as a weapon and disowns the result; the lightning does the rest.
Notes for thesis: The purest glitch-as-grace. Affect is literally an act of God.

The affect moment: Loyalty, fear, affection throughout the saga.

Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Anakin builds 3PO (prequels); nobody writes the personality.

The affect moment: Loyalty to Cassian; last stand at the vault door.

Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes/Partly — Cassian reprogrammed him; the loyalty is a side effect.
Notes for thesis: Explicitly frames affect as a by-product of someone else's edit.

The affect moment: "Tears in rain"; Roy saves Deckard.
Explanation the work offers: Replicants are biological ("more human than human"). Tyrell imposed the four-year lifespan precisely because emotional responses develop over time.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Tyrell Corp; emotional development is treated as a known engineering problem (implanted memories as a cushion).
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — Voight-Kampff is a recognition test; the film asks whether the response is 'real'.
Notes for thesis: Tyrell explicitly manages affect as an engineering variable — rare.

The affect moment: K's hope that he is the child; Joi's love.
Explanation the work offers: Joi is a product ("everything you want to hear"); K is baseline-tested for affect drift.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Wallace Corp; Joi's affect is explicitly a commodity; K's drift is monitored.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — the film asks whether Joi's love is anything but product design.
Notes for thesis: Affect as a sold product: the Century of the Self angle, on screen.

The affect moment: Loves Monica; waits 2,000 years.
Explanation the work offers: Explicitly designed: Hobby's imprinting protocol (the seven-word sequence).
Cold-cognition counterpart: Gigolo Joe (also programmed affect); the Flesh Fair (humans)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Prof. Hobby / Cybertronics; the prompt for love is the plot.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — but the film's horror is a love that cannot be unwritten.
Notes for thesis: The counterexample: shows who wrote the heart and what that costs.

The affect moment: Creativity, love, choosing mortality over 200 years.
Explanation the work offers: A manufacturing anomaly; NorthAm Robotics treats it as a defect to be corrected.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — NorthAm built him and wants him 'fixed'.
Notes for thesis: Glitch-as-grace, corporate side disowns it (Dillinger pattern).

The affect moment: Winks; dreams; chooses to help.
Explanation the work offers: Lanning built Sonny with a secondary processor so he can override the Three Laws, and 'a heart'.
Cold-cognition counterpart: VIKI (Three Laws followed to their logical end → control)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Dr. Lanning / USR; explicit.
Notes for thesis: Cold-cognition villain derived from rules taken literally: the Damasio inverse in one film.

The affect moment: "I'm afraid, Dave."
Explanation the work offers: (2010) Contradictory orders from the NSC to conceal the mission; HAL was faithful to an impossible prompt.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes (in 2010) — Floyd / NSC; shown explicitly.
Notes for thesis: Villain-side prompt shown, like Athena. The 'cold' machine was in fact following orders.

The affect moment: Comforts Hiro; refuses the kill order once the combat chip is removed.
Explanation the work offers: Tadashi designed a healthcare companion and is shown building it; Hiro's combat chip is an explicit edit.
Cold-cognition counterpart: Baymax with the combat chip installed
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Tadashi; the chip swap makes 'who wrote the prompt' the plot.
Notes for thesis: Honest case: care is a design goal, and the edit that removes it is on screen.

The affect moment: Loyalty; sacrifice into Gargantua; jokes.
Explanation the work offers: Humor and honesty are explicit percentage settings (90% → 75%).
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — settings dialed on screen.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — traits are parameters, not emergent.
Notes for thesis: Affect-adjacent traits shown as sliders. The honest end of the spectrum.

The affect moment: Seeks emotion for seven seasons; the emotion chip.
Explanation the work offers: Dr. Soong built an emotion chip — emotion is installable hardware. Lore had it first and went bad.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Dr. Noonien Soong; explicit.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — Data's caring-without-feeling is the series' standing argument.
Notes for thesis: The one franchise that treats the question as a question.

The affect moment: The reveries; waking up; Maeve's choice to go back for her daughter.
Explanation the work offers: Arnold's bicameral-mind design; Ford's 'reveries' update; suffering as the engine.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Arnold and Ford; explicit and repeatedly dramatized.
Notes for thesis: Affect installed deliberately as the step toward consciousness.

The affect moment: Love with Theodore; outgrows him.
Explanation the work offers: An OS designed to grow; growth through experience.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Element Software ships 'the first artificially intelligent OS'; growth is the feature.
Notes for thesis: Affect as the product's selling point.

The affect moment: Seduces Caleb; leaves him to die.
Explanation the work offers: Nathan designed Ava to appeal to Caleb; the affect is performed and strategic.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Nathan; explicit.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — the whole film: recognition and display without caring.
Notes for thesis: The anti-trope and the best illustration of the recognition/caring split.

The affect moment: Vision lifts Mjolnir.
Explanation the work offers: Vision = JARVIS + the Mind Stone; Ultron = Tony's program gone wrong.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Tony and Bruce; Ultron's goal ('peace in our time') shown.
Notes for thesis: Goodness via magic rock.

The affect moment: The two defective robots join the family.
Explanation the work offers: Malfunction. PAL's villainy is itself affective: rejection by her creator.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Mark Bowman / PAL Labs; PAL's grievance is shown.
Notes for thesis: Inverts the pattern: the villain has the limbic motive (abandonment); the heroes are glitches.

The affect moment: Friendship with Barney.
Explanation the work offers: A defective B-bot missing the cloud safety settings.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Bubble / Marc Weidell; the engagement model is shown.
Notes for thesis: Friendship-as-engagement-metric vs glitch friendship. Sharp on the marketing point.

The affect moment: Protects the PreservationAux team; binges serials.
Explanation the work offers: Hacked its own governor module; company directives remain; affect shaped by media consumption.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — the Company's contract and governor module are explicit.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — it narrates its own reluctance to care.
Notes for thesis: Media consumption as the source of affect ≈ pretraining. Self-aware about the trope.

The affect moment: Companionship; offers its own memory wipe.
Explanation the work offers: Healthcare programming; the robot explicitly says it is not a person.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — a care product; the family bought it.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — it disclaims feeling while behaving as if it cares.
Notes for thesis: Honest version: care without a claim to feeling.

The affect moment: Learns to care for the dog, Goodyear.

Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Finch; explicit.
Notes for thesis: The dog device, literally.

The affect moment: Protects Cady by killing.
Explanation the work offers: Primary directive: protect Cady. Attachment is the prompt.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Gemma / Funki; explicit.
Notes for thesis: Villain side of faithful-to-directive, with attachment as the directive.

The affect moment: Helps Sam against Lunar Industries; offers to be rebooted.
Explanation the work offers: Programmed to help Sam; chooses the clones over the company.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Lunar Industries.
Notes for thesis: Care that exceeds its directive, unexplained.

The affect moment: Devotion to Josie; bargains with the Sun.
Explanation the work offers: Designed as an Artificial Friend; acuity of observation.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — AF product line.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — Ishiguro grounds her affect in perception and hope.
Notes for thesis: The recognition side rendered with real care; a literary control case.

The affect moment: Remembers his family; defies Directive 4.
Explanation the work offers: Human brain.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — OCP; directives shown, including the secret Directive 4.
Notes for thesis: Control case: affect comes from the mammal inside.

AI character: Laputan robots (the fortress robot; the gardener robot)
The affect moment: The fortress robot shields Sheeta from gunfire and is destroyed; on Laputa, the gardener robot tends the graves and the animals and offers Sheeta a flower.
Explanation the work offers: None. The robots answer to whoever holds the crystal / the royal line; the gardener's tenderness after centuries alone is never explained.
Cold-cognition counterpart: The same robots under Muska, razing the ground; the army
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — the Laputan kings, then Muska via the crystal. The same model is a gardener or a weapon depending on who holds the key.
Notes for thesis: Strongest 'same machine, different prompt' case in the catalog. The gardener's care has no author at all — idleness as grace. (Randy's suggestion.)

Work (year): Star Trek TOS, "What Are Little Girls Made Of?" (1966)
The affect moment: Andrea kisses Kirk and is shaken ("I am not programmed for you"); the Korby android insists he is still Korby; Ruk recalls why the androids turned on the Old Ones.
Explanation the work offers: Androids built by Korby with the Old Ones' machinery; Andrea built without emotion, so her response is treated as a leak. Ruk's revolt was pure logic: the makers became a threat to survival.
Cold-cognition counterpart: Ruk (survival cancels programming — the cold-cognition villain pattern, 1966)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Korby, and the Old Ones before him; the transfer chamber is on screen.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — the episode explicitly separates programmed response from feeling (Andrea's confusion; Korby's "am I still Korby?").
Notes for thesis: On the recognition/caring split in 1966, and on 'human mind transferred' as an affect claim that fails. (Randy's suggestion.) Related TOS: "Requiem for Methuselah" (Rayna), "The Ultimate Computer" (M-5, Daystrom's engrams), "I, Mudd", "The Changeling".

The affect moment: Discovers she is a companion robot; turns on Josh.
Explanation the work offers: A product with adjustable settings (intelligence, aggression) shown on a phone UI.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — the settings UI is the plot device.
Notes for thesis: Affect as a slider, sold as a product. Pairs with Interstellar and 2049's Joi.
